planting.note: Sow seed in fall or plant divisions/rooted rosettes in a gritty, sharply drained, neutral to alkaline scree or trough mix in full sun; this tight cushion-former resents winter wet far more than cold, so tuck it where rain runs off quickly and top-dress with grit to keep the crown dry.

directions: Plant in a lean, gritty, sharply drained scree or trough mix in full sun, keeping the tight rosettes elevated slightly on grit so foliage never sits in standing moisture. This true limestone-cliff alpine from the mountains of Europe forms a dense, hard, hummock-like cushion of tiny overlapping evergreen rosettes studded in earliest spring with small four-petaled bright-yellow flowers held just above the foliage on short stems. It is a classic trough and tufa plant, valued as much for its neat year-round cushion form as for its bloom, and needs winter protection from prolonged wet more than from cold. Top-dress annually with fresh grit around the crown to discourage rot and keep the cushion tight.

planting.note: Plant offsets or nursery divisions in spring into a gritty, humus-enriched, sharply drained scree or trough mix in full sun to light shade; the mother rosette naturally dies back after producing stolon-borne offsets, so leave the new baby rosettes in place to root and expand the mat rather than removing them.

directions: Plant in a gritty, humus-enriched, sharply drained scree, trough, or raised-bed mix in full sun to light shade, sheltered from the worst summer heat. This Himalayan rock jasmine spreads by short leafy stolons, each tipped with a small silver-hairy rosette, gradually knitting together into a loose silvery mat that is smothered in late spring by rounded clusters of pink flowers with a small yellow-and-white eye, held just above the foliage on short stems. It is one of the easier androsace species for garden cultivation, tolerating somewhat more moisture and summer warmth than the tight cushion species, but still needs winter drainage and a lean root run to avoid rot. Established mats are best left largely undisturbed, dividing only to propagate or to rejuvenate an aging patch.

planting.note: Surface-sow fine seed in spring directly into gritty, gap-filled crevices of a dry stone wall, scree, or paving joint in full sun to partial shade; fairy foxglove germinates readily and self-sows freely once established, so a single planting soon colonizes nearby crevices on its own.

directions: Tuck plants or seed into a lean, gritty, well-drained crevice, dry stone wall, or gravel path in full sun to partial shade. This short-lived Pyrenean and Alpine wildflower forms small semi-evergreen rosettes of hairy, toothed leaves topped from late spring into summer by short spikes of tiny snapdragon-like flowers in shades of magenta-pink, rose, or white. It is one of the easiest true alpines to grow, thriving in the poor, gritty conditions of a wall crevice or gravel path where it self-sows readily and moves itself into cracks and gaps year after year, effectively behaving as a long-lived colony even though individual plants are short-lived. Shear off spent flower spikes to tidy the rosettes and to moderate (though rarely stop) self-seeding.

planting.note: Sow seed in spring in lean, gritty, alkaline to neutral, sharply drained soil in full sun; Persian stonecress dislikes root disturbance and transplants poorly once established, so sow in place or set out young pot-grown plants while still small.

directions: Plant in lean, gritty, sharply drained, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Persian stonecress forms a woody-based, blue-gray-leaved subshrub that becomes smothered from late spring into early summer in dense, rounded clusters of small, clear-pink, four-petaled flowers held above the foliage in a soft haze of color. Native to the rocky, sun-baked slopes of the eastern Mediterranean and Middle East, it is exceptionally heat- and drought-tolerant and, unlike many alpines, actually prefers hot, dry summers to cool, moist ones. Shear lightly after flowering to keep the mound compact and to encourage denser regrowth, but avoid rich soil or heavy watering, both of which shorten its lifespan and cause lank, floppy growth.

planting.note: Sow fresh seed in fall and leave exposed to winter cold, since a cold stratification period is needed to break dormancy; plant into a humus-rich but sharply drained, slightly acidic to neutral scree or rock garden bed in full sun to light shade, and expect several years before the mat is large enough to flower well.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, sharply drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to light shade, watering regularly during the growing season but never letting the crown sit wet over winter. This iconic European alpine forms a low, spreading mat of glossy, dark-green, evergreen rosettes from which enormous trumpet-shaped flowers of the most intense deep sky-blue rise on very short stems in late spring, often marked inside with green spots at the throat, in stunning proportion to the tiny plant. It can be temperamental in cultivation away from its native limestone alpine meadows, sometimes sulking or refusing to flower for a year or two after transplanting, and appreciates a cool root run and steady moisture through summer despite needing sharp winter drainage. Top-dress with grit and avoid disturbing established clumps, which slowly increase in flower production as the mat matures.

planting.note: Sow seed in fall and expose to winter cold for germination the following spring, or plant nursery-grown cushions into a gritty, sharply drained scree or trough mix in full sun; moss campion is extremely slow-growing from seed, often taking several years to form a cushion of flowering size.

directions: Plant in a lean, gritty, sharply drained scree or trough mix in full sun, choosing a cool site that avoids prolonged summer heat. This circumpolar and high-alpine wildflower forms one of the tightest, hardest cushions in the plant world, a dense dome of tiny overlapping mossy leaves that can live for decades, dotted in late spring and early summer with small, stemless, deep-pink to rose flowers sitting directly on the cushion surface. It is extremely slow-growing and long-lived, native to some of the harshest, most exposed alpine and arctic tundra on the planet, and performs best in cool-summer rock gardens with sharp drainage; it is often disappointing or short-lived in hot, humid regions. Avoid rich soil, overhead watering, and root disturbance, all of which can quickly rot the tightly packed cushion.
